recipes.name: Citronfromage

items.name: Eggs
items.description: 3, separated — they stay raw, so buy fresh ones you trust

items.name: Lemon zest
items.description: of 1 of the lemons, finely grated

items.name: Double cream
items.description: 400 ml — 250 ml folded in, the rest for the top

recipes.description:
The dessert that outlived every food fashion because Danish grandmothers simply refused to stop making it. Citronfromage is 1950s dinner-party engineering — raw eggs, real lemon, gelatine and air — and made properly it is still one of the best things you can do to a lemon.

## 1. Soak

1. Put the gelatine sheets in plenty of cold water and leave them 10 minutes while you work. They should go completely limp.

## 2. Whisk the yolks

1. Whisk the egg yolks with the sugar until pale, thick and ribbon-like — a good few minutes, and worth every one, because this is where the sugar dissolves and the fromage gets its body.
2. Whisk in the lemon juice and the lemon zest.

## 3. Marry the gelatine — where it lives or dies

1. Lift out the sheets, squeeze them, and melt them in a small bowl set over hot water; they need barely a minute.
2. Whisk two or three spoonfuls of the lemon mixture into the warm gelatine first, then pour that back into the bowl in a thin stream, whisking constantly. Hot gelatine poured straight into a cold mixture sets on contact into rubbery threads, and no amount of whisking brings it back.

## 4. Fold

1. Whip the egg whites to soft peaks in a spotless bowl, and separately whip 250 ml of the cream to soft peaks.
2. When the lemon base has just started to thicken, fold in the whites, then the cream, keeping as much air as you can. Fold too early and it separates into a jelly layer under a foam layer — some families insist they prefer the layers, and you may believe them or not.

## 5. Set and crown

1. Pour into a glass bowl or individual glasses and refrigerate at least 4 hours, better overnight.
2. Just before serving, whip the remaining cream and spread it over the top. The cream lid is not decoration; citronfromage without it is simply not served, and every grandmother agrees on this one.

recipes.name: Rødgrød med fløde

items.name: Redcurrants
items.description: 500 g, stripped from their stalks (fresh or frozen)

items.name: Sugar
items.description: 150 g, plus a spoonful for the surface

items.name: Water
items.description: 200 ml, plus 3 tbsp cold for the starch

items.name: Double cream
items.description: 250 ml, cold and unwhipped, for the table

recipes.description:
The dish Danes hand to foreigners as a pronunciation test, then happily eat while the guest is still trying. However you manage the name, rødgrød med fløde is red summer berries thickened with potato starch to a soft wobble — never glue — with cold cream poured over at the table.

## 1. Simmer the fruit

1. Bring the redcurrants and the 200 ml of water to the boil and simmer 3-4 minutes until the berries burst.
2. Add the strawberries, the raspberries if using, and the sugar, and simmer 3-4 minutes more. The fruit should be soft but still recognisably fruit, not jam.

## 2. Thicken — wobble, not glue

1. Stir the potato starch smooth with the 3 tbsp of cold water.
2. Take the pan off the heat, stir the slurry in, then return it to the lowest heat just until the grød thickens and turns glossy and translucent — a matter of moments. Potato starch that is allowed to boil turns ropey and gluey, and everyone at the table will know exactly what happened.
3. Pour into a serving bowl and sprinkle the spoonful of sugar over the surface so it does not form a skin.

## 3. Chill

1. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 2 hours. It should set to a spoonable wobble, not a jelly.

## 4. Med fløde

1. Serve cold with the cream — cold, unwhipped, in a jug — poured over by each person at the table, never stirred in beforehand.
2. Having made it, you have earned the right to ask a foreign guest to say the name before they get the jug.

---

recipes.name: Pandekager

items.name: Milk
items.description: 500 ml, plus a splash if needed

items.name: Sugar
items.description: 2 tbsp for the batter, plus plenty for rolling

items.name: Butter
items.description: 50 g — half melted into the batter, half for the pan

recipes.description:
Thinner than an American pancake, a shade sturdier than a French crêpe, and rolled around plain sugar. Two laws apply: the batter rests, and the first pancake — always wrong, always — belongs to the cook, eaten standing at the stove.

## 1. Make the batter

1. Whisk the flour, sugar and salt with half the milk to a thick, completely lump-free paste; lumps get caught now or never.
2. Whisk in the eggs, then the rest of the milk, the vanilla and half the butter, melted. The batter should be thin, like single cream.

## 2. Rest — the part people skip

1. Leave it 30 minutes at room temperature. The flour swells, the bubbles settle, and the pancakes stop tearing when you flip them. Skipping the rest is why the first three fail instead of just the first.

## 3. Fry thin

1. Heat a good frying pan over medium-high and brush it with a little of the remaining butter.
2. Pour in a small ladleful and immediately tilt and swirl so it just coats the base. If it will not swirl thin, loosen the batter with a splash of milk.
3. Cook 1-2 minutes until the underside is lacy gold and the top has set, flip, and give it 30 seconds more. Re-butter the pan every two or three pancakes.
4. The first one goes to the cook, per law. Stack the rest on a plate, where they keep each other warm and soft.

## 4. Roll

1. Lay a line of sugar across each pancake and roll it into a tube. Purists stop exactly there.
2. For the ambitious: a stripe of strawberry jam before rolling, or a scoop of vanilla ice cream folded inside while the pancake is still warm. Count on more per person than seems reasonable.

---

recipes.name: Øllebrød

items.name: Rye bread
items.description: 300 g stale dark rye (rugbrød), torn or cubed

items.name: Milk
items.description: cold, the weekday alternative to the cream

recipes.description:
The most Danish instruction in food: do not throw out the rugbrød. Stale rye simmered with malt beer into a dark porridge sounds like a punishment and tastes — genuinely, ask anyone who grew up on it — closer to warm chocolate, which is why restaurants with tasting menus now serve what frugal households never stopped making.

## 1. Soak overnight

1. Tear or cube the bread into the pan it will cook in, pour over the water and the malt beer, and press it under the surface.
2. Cover and leave it overnight on the counter. A few hours will do at a pinch, but overnight is both the tradition and the texture.

## 2. Simmer smooth

1. Set the pan over low heat and simmer 10-15 minutes, whisking often, until the bread collapses into a thick, glossy, dark porridge. It catches on the bottom like every porridge, so keep the whisk moving along it.
2. Whisk hard for a rustic texture, or blend and sieve it if you want the silk the restaurants sell.
3. Sweeten with the sugar to taste and stir in the lemon zest. It should land malty, dark and gently sweet-sour; loosen with a splash of water if it stands too stiff.

## 3. Serve

1. Ladle it hot into bowls and top with the softly whipped cream — or pour cold milk around it, which is the honest weekday version.
2. Eat it while it is hot, and be quietly surprised, like everyone before you.

---
